prompt:
In Python, which call is likely to take the longest?

```python
import re
p = re.compile(r"(a+)+$")
A = p.match("a" * 12)
B = p.match("a" * 12 + "!")
C = p.match("!")
D = p.match("")
```

options.explanation: With 12 a characters and nothing else, the first greedy attempt succeeds.
Correct. The failing suffix forces repeated attempts; the 12 a characters have 2,048 possible nonempty-block decompositions. No fixed wall-clock time is claimed.
The first character is not an a, so `a+` fails immediately and there is nothing to backtrack into.
An empty string fails `a+` at once; no choices exist to explore.

workedExample: A succeeds on its first greedy attempt. B fails after exploring ambiguous splits; 12 characters have 2,048 (two to the power eleven) decompositions into positive-length blocks. C and D fail immediately. The smaller runnable example illustrates the behavior without requiring an expensive 30-character failing match. Successful matches in other patterns can also require extensive backtracking.

link.title: Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast — Russ Cox

prompt: Which engine guarantees matching time linear in the length of the input? Consider a single search with a fixed pattern and the standard APIs listed.

options.explanation: Python's `re` is a backtracking engine. `(a+)+$` is exponential in it.
Java's standard matcher uses backtracking and does not document a general input-linear matching guarantee. Optimisations can change the behaviour of individual patterns.
Correct. Go's documentation states it is "guaranteed to run in time linear in the size of the input", because it simulates the automaton rather than searching paths.
PCRE's main matcher is backtracking (it supports backreferences and recursion), so it has no linear guarantee.

workedExample: Go regexp documents a bound linear in input length. Python re, Java’s standard matcher and PCRE’s default matcher do not offer that general guarantee. Production libraries can mix methods; PCRE2 also offers a separate DFA-style matcher, and recent Ruby versions memoize many patterns.

link.title: Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast — Russ Cox

prompt: An unmemoised backtracker full-matches `(a+)+` against a long a-run followed by b. Why can one extra a cause much more work?

options.explanation: The pattern still rejects b; the suffix only exposes failing alternatives.
The symbols remain a and b.

options.text: It adds another gap that can split or join repetitions
options.explanation: Correct. Each new cut-or-no-cut choice creates more decompositions of the same run.

options.text: It makes the NFA gain states while matching
options.explanation: The compiled pattern is fixed; the repeated exploration grows.

workedExample: The same a-run can be divided among inner repetitions in many ways. A final b makes each complete division fail. The backtracker revisits these alternatives unless optimisations or memoisation prevent it. Set simulation merges equivalent active states instead of tracking every division separately.
